journal.title: How to read an INCI list without googling everything
journal.text: A few simple ways to make sense of a skincare label.
body: INCI is the international naming system for cosmetic ingredients. It helps you compare product formulas, no matter what language is on the packaging. Start with the full list, not just the ingredient highlighted on the front.

Ingredients present above 1% are generally listed in descending order. Those at lower concentrations may appear in a different order. The position alone cannot tell you an exact percentage or how well a formula works.

Look at the overall base—water, oils and humectants—then check for any fragrance or ingredients you know your skin reacts to. A long chemical name does not automatically mean an ingredient is harmful, and natural origin does not guarantee a product will suit everyone.

If your skin is sensitive, introduce new products gradually and follow the directions. Stop use if irritation occurs and seek professional advice when needed. This note is for reading labels, not a substitute for personalized care.

journal.title: Double cleansing: when do you really need it?
journal.text: Who might benefit from two steps—and who may only need one.
body: Double cleansing means two evening steps: first, a product to remove long-wear makeup or water-resistant SPF; then, a gentle cleanser. It is an option for a specific need, not a required routine for everyone.
Use an oil or balm for the first step according to its directions. Some formulas work best on dry skin, others on damp skin. Avoid prolonged rubbing and rinse thoroughly.
For the second step, a small amount of gentle cleanser is usually enough. Hot water, brushes and harsh scrubbing can add to dryness. Your skin should not feel persistently tight after washing.
If one cleanser removes your sunscreen and makeup comfortably, a second step may not be necessary. Pay attention to your skin and the product directions; simplify your routine if irritation occurs.

journal.title: Ceramides: part of your skin's protective barrier
journal.text: What they do and how they fit into a simple routine.
body: Ceramides are lipids naturally found in the outer layer of the skin. Along with other lipids, they play a role in the skin barrier, which helps limit moisture loss.
In skincare, ceramides are used in moisturizing formulas designed to support the skin barrier. The full formula and how your skin responds matter more than a single word on the label.
A ceramide moisturizer can follow a gentle cleanse and a water-based serum, if that order works for your routine. In the morning, finish with a sunscreen suited to you.
Persistent stinging, cracking or pronounced flaking is a reason to seek advice from a dermatologist. A cosmetic cream is not intended to diagnose or treat a skin condition.
